title: Effects of velocity-based strength training versus percentage-based strength training on technical error rates in collegiate lion dance athletes: A randomized controlled trial
content:
by Mu Yuan Yang

Background

Lion dance is a Chinese intangible cultural heritage that demands exceptional strength, explosive power, and movement precision. Velocity-based training has shown benefits for general athletic performance, but its effects on sport-specific technical performance in traditional sports remain unclear.

Objective

To compare the effects of velocity-based training and percentage-based training on technical error rates in collegiate lion dance athletes.

Methods

Thirty collegiate lion dance athletes were recruited and randomly assigned in fixed head–tail pairs to a velocity-based training group (VBT, n = 10), a percentage-based training group (PBT, n = 10), or a regular-training control group (CON, n = 10). Both training groups completed a 6-week intervention (3 sessions per week) consisting of back squats (tail athletes) and strict overhead presses (head athletes). The VBT group used real-time velocity feedback with a 10% velocity-loss threshold; the PBT group followed a progressive percentage-based loading protocol (50–70% 1RM). All three groups continued the team's regular lion dance technical and conditioning training. Two blinded assessors evaluated sitting-on-shoulder and standing-on-leg technical error rates weekly. The unit of analysis for both primary technical outcomes was the head–tail pair (n = 5 pairs per group; 15 pairs total). Maximal strength (squat 1RM, strict press 1RM) was measured at baseline and post-intervention as a secondary outcome. The principal between-group analyses were analysis of covariance at each follow-up time point with the baseline error rate as covariate, supported by a 3 × 7 mixed-design repeated-measures ANOVA evaluating the Group × Time interaction. Significance testing of baseline imbalances among randomized groups was not performed, in accordance with current methodological recommendations.

Results

All 30 participants completed the intervention. Statistically significant Group × Time interactions were found for both sitting-on-shoulder (F(12, 72) = 1.99, P = 0.037, partial η2 = 0.249) and standing-on-leg (F(12, 72) = 4.24, P < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.414) error rates. ANCOVA-adjusted between-group comparisons indicated that the VBT group reduced sitting-on-shoulder error rate significantly more than the CON group from Week 3 onward and significantly more than the PBT group from Week 5 (adjusted mean difference at Week 6 vs CON: −35.5 percentage points, 95% CI: −50.6 to −20.4; vs PBT: −19.5 percentage points, 95% CI: −34.6 to −4.4). The corresponding pattern was observed for standing-on-leg error rate (adjusted mean difference at Week 6 vs CON: −36.0 percentage points, 95% CI: −48.6 to −23.4; vs PBT: −18.4 percentage points, 95% CI: −31.2 to −5.7). For secondary maximal-strength outcomes, the Group × Time interactions were statistically significant for both squat 1RM (F(4, 24) = 14.47, P < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.707) and strict press 1RM (F(4, 24) = 9.45, P < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.612). Post-hoc analyses showed that VBT and PBT produced significantly larger pre-to-post 1RM gains than CON; VBT and PBT differed marginally on squat (mean difference +2.72 kg, P = 0.049) and not significantly on strict press (+0.70 kg, P = 0.706).

Conclusion

Among these collegiate lion-dance athletes, velocity-based training produced significantly greater between-group reductions in sitting-on-shoulder and standing-on-leg error rates than continued regular lion-dance training alone, and a significantly greater reduction than percentage-based training from the fifth week of the intervention. Both strength-training regimens produced significantly larger maximal-strength gains than continued regular training, but VBT and PBT were largely comparable in strength gains despite VBT's substantially greater technical advantage over PBT, suggesting that the technical-performance advantage of velocity-based training is not adequately explained by between-method differences in maximal-strength gains. Larger, multi-center trials are needed to confirm these preliminary findings.
